text: Michael Stanley Dukakis (/dʊˈkɑːkɪs/ duu-KAH-kiss; born November 3, 1933) is an American politician and lawyer who served as governor of Massachusetts from 1975 to 1979 and from 1983 to 1991, making him the longest-serving governor in Massachusetts history and the second Greek-American governor in U.S. history, after Spiro Agnew. Born in Brookline, Massachusetts, to Greek immigrants, Dukakis attended Swarthmore College, where he earned a Bachelor of Arts in political science in 1955, before enlisting in the United States Army from 1955 to 1957. After completing his military service, he received a J.D. from Harvard Law School in 1960. He began his political career as a town meeting member in Brookline and served in the Massachusetts House of Representatives from 1963 to 1971. He won the 1974 gubernatorial election, defeating incumbent Francis Sargent, and pledged a "lead pipe guarantee" of no new taxes and a dismantling of the powerful Metropolitan District Commission (MDC), though he failed to achieve these goals. After losing his 1978 bid for re-nomination to Edward J. King, he defeated King in the 1982 Democratic primary and served as governor from 1983 to 1991, presiding over a period of economic growth known as the "Massachusetts Miracle." Building on his popularity, Dukakis sought the Democratic presidential nomination in 1988, prevailing in the primaries and being formally nominated at the 1988 Democratic National Convention. He chose Senator Lloyd Bentsen of Texas as his running mate, while the Republicans nominated George H. W. Bush and Senator Dan Quayle. Dukakis made history as the first Greek-American and Aromanian presidential candidate, the first Greek Orthodox major-party nominee, and the first major-party nominee with ancestry outside Europe. Although he lost the election, carrying only ten states and Washington, D.C., he improved on the Democratic performances in the previous two elections. After the election, Dukakis announced he would not seek another term as governor and left office in 1991. Since the death of Jimmy Carter in 2024, Dukakis is the oldest living presidential nominee. Since leaving office, he has served on the board of directors for Amtrak and taught political science at Northeastern University and UCLA. He was considered a potential Senate appointee in 2009 following Ted Kennedy's death, though Governor Deval Patrick selected Paul G. Kirk. In 2012, Dukakis supported Elizabeth Warren in her Senate campaign and in the 2020 Democratic presidential primaries. Dukakis's father, Panos, was a Greek immigrant from Edremit in Turkey who settled in Lowell, Massachusetts, and graduated from Harvard Medical School in 1924, working as an obstetrician. His mother, Euterpe (née Boukis), was born in Larissa to Aromanian parents from Vrysochori and emigrated to Haverhill, Massachusetts, in 1913. Dukakis attended Brookline High School, where he was an honor student and a member of basketball, baseball, tennis, and cross-country teams, and ran the Boston Marathon as a 17-year-old senior. He married Katherine "Kitty" Dickson in 1963, and they remained together until her death in March 2025. Dukakis has a brother, Stelian, who was three years his elder; Stelian suffered a mental breakdown and attempted suicide when Michael was seventeen, was institutionalized for years, and later became a teacher, professor, and assistant city manager. He unsuccessfully attempted to sabotage Michael's 1964 campaign by distributing anti-Michael pamphlets and ran for the Brookline Board of Selectmen twice and once in 1972 for the Massachusetts House of Representatives as a Republican before dying in 1973 after being struck by a car while cycling. Dukakis served four terms in the Massachusetts House of Representatives between 1962 and 1970, ran unsuccessfully for Attorney General in 1966, and was the Democratic nominee for lieutenant governor in 1970 on a ticket with Boston mayor Kevin White, but the ticket lost the gubernatorial election. After losing the lieutenant governor race, he returned to the private sector, practicing law at Hill and Barlow. During his first term as governor, he commuted the sentences of 21 first-degree murderers and 23 second-degree murderers and hosted President Gerald Ford and Queen Elizabeth II during their 1976 visits to Boston. He gained recognition for working during the Blizzard of 1978 and for exonerating Sacco and Vanzetti in 1977. His first term was undermined by backlash over high sales and property taxes, leading to his defeat in the 1978 primary by Edward J. King, a decision that his wife Kitty called "a public death." After that, he taught at Harvard University's John F. Kennedy School of Government and published the book State and Cities: The Massachusetts Experience in 1980. In 1982, after making peace with the Democratic Party, the MDC, state police, and public employee unions, he defeated King in the Democratic primary and went on to defeat Republican John Winthrop Sears in the November election, with John Kerry elected lieutenant governor on the same ballot. As governor, he presided over a high-tech boom and prosperity, earning a reputation as a 'technocrat,' and was voted the most effective governor by the National Governors Association in 1986. Residents of Boston and its surrounding areas remember him for improvements to the city's mass transit system, especially train and bus renovations, and he was known for riding the subway to work every day. In 1988, Dukakis and Rosabeth Moss Kanter co-authored Creating the Future: the Massachusetts Comeback and Its Promise for America, an examination of the "Massachusetts Miracle." He won the Democratic nomination in 1988, receiving 2,877 out of 4,105 delegates, and was pro-choice on abortion. He made history as the first non-Western European American major-party nominee and the only major presidential nominee with ancestry from outside Northwestern Europe until Barack Obama's nomination in 2008. He enjoyed strong support among Greek Americans, with the Associated Press reporting an "outpouring of pride" in April 1988, especially among older generations. Dukakis emphasized his working-class background as the son of impoverished immigrants and his fluency in Greek and other languages, using Neil Diamond's "America" as the campaign theme song. His reserved and stoic nature led to criticism, with him being referred to as "Zorba the Clerk," though he performed well in the first presidential debate, with The New York Times noting that analysts generally agreed he outperformed George H. W. Bush. In the second debate, his performance was poor and reinforced his image as cold. During the campaign, concerns about his mental health arose when he refused to release his full medical history, with persistent suggestions of past psychiatric treatment; President Reagan referred to him as an "invalid" at a White House press conference, and journalist Robert Novak revealed in the 2008 film Boogie Man: The Lee Atwater Story that Lee Atwater personally tried to spread these rumors. Editors at The Washington Times contributed to the rumors with a story headlined "Dukakis Kin Hints at Sessions," which was later corrected to show the full quote was "It's possible, but I doubt it." Dukakis faced criticism over capital punishment, the pledge of allegiance in schools, and a photograph of him in a tank during a 1988 photo op at the General Dynamics Land Systems plant in Sterling Heights, Michigan. The image, intended to portray him as a strong commander-in-chief, backfired when he was photographed without a helmet as the tank exited the garage, though most photographers captured him wearing a helmet during a high-speed pass. The image was ridiculed by Bush and the media, with a poll showing 25 percent of respondents were less likely to support him, and footage was used in a Bush campaign ad during the World Series. The Dukakis campaign responded with a 60-second ad featuring a television set playing the Bush ad being flicked off by a finger revealed to be Dukakis, who proclaimed he was fed up with "George Bush's negative TV ads," a tactic later labeled "pin-the-tail-on-the-donkey advertising." The phrase "Dukakis in the tank" remains a shorthand for backfired public relations efforts. In 2008, when asked about the photograph, Dukakis said "Should I have been in the tank? Probably not, in retrospect. But these days when people ask me, 'Did you get here in a tank?' I always respond by saying, 'No, and I've never thrown up all over the Japanese prime minister.'" The Dukakis/Bentsen ticket lost the 1988 election by a decisive margin in the Electoral College to George H. W. Bush and Dan Quayle, carrying only ten states and Washington, D.C.

Footage of Michael Dukakis in a tank was used in a television ad by the Bush campaign that aired during the World Series. In response, the Dukakis campaign produced a 60-second ad showing a television set playing Bush's ad, which is flicked off the screen by a finger later revealed to be Dukakis as he declares he is fed up with "George Bush's negative TV ads"; this "pin-the-tail-on-the-donkey" style advertising only drew further attention to the tank ride. The phrase "Dukakis in the tank" has since become shorthand for backfired public relations moments. In 2008, when asked about the image, Dukakis said he probably should not have been in the tank, but he now responds to questions about it by saying, "No, and I've never thrown up all over the Japanese prime minister." The Dukakis/Bentsen ticket lost the election by a decisive margin in the Electoral College to George H. W. Bush and Dan Quayle, winning only 10 states and the District of Columbia. Many believed the loss stemmed from Dukakis's failure to campaign nationally and his delayed response to Bush's attack campaign, which caused his 17-point lead in opinion polls to vanish as Bush defined the campaign's issues. Dukakis has stated that not responding to the Bush attack campaign was a "pretty dumb decision." Despite the loss, his performance improved over previous Democratic candidates, with Bush winning a majority of the popular vote but Dukakis's margin of loss (7.8%) being narrower than Jimmy Carter's in 1980 (9.7%) or Walter Mondale's in 1984 (18.2%), and earning 41.8 million votes nationally. Dukakis achieved strong results in states that had previously voted Republican, including New York (the second-largest state by electoral votes at the time), Rhode Island, Hawaii, Massachusetts, Oregon, and Washington, and won Iowa by 10 points—a state that had voted Republican in the previous five presidential elections. His popular vote share in South Dakota (46.51%), Kansas (42.56%), Oklahoma (41.28%), Wyoming (38.01%), and Idaho (36.01%) would not be matched by any subsequent Democratic presidential candidate. Although Dukakis reduced Republican dominance in the Midwest, he failed to challenge the growing GOP strength in the South, losing most Southern states by wide margins—Bush's popular vote margins exceeded 15% in most—though Dukakis carried most of the southern-central parishes of Louisiana, which was his best Southern popular vote margin. His second-lowest Southern margin was in Texas, where four overwhelmingly Mexican-American counties in South Texas delivered more than 81% of the vote to Dukakis, and these counties ranked among his top five nationally. In 2008, Dukakis stated during an interview with Katie Couric that he "owe[d] the American people an apology" because "if I had beaten the old man [i.e. George H. W. Bush], we never would have heard of the kid [i.e. George W. Bush], and we wouldn't be in this mess." His final two years as governor were marked by increased criticism of his policies and significant tax increases to address the economic effects of the U.S. economy's "soft landing" at the end of the 1980s and the 1990 recession, leading him to announce in early 1989 that he would not seek reelection to a fourth term. After leaving office, Dukakis served on the board of directors for Amtrak and became a professor of political science at Northeastern University, a visiting professor at Loyola Marymount University, and a visiting professor in the Department of Public Policy at the Luskin School of Public Affairs at UCLA. He retired from teaching by 2021. Along with other notable Greek-Americans, he is a founding member of The Next Generation Initiative, a leadership program for student involvement in public affairs. In November 2008, Northeastern named its Center for Urban and Regional Policy after Michael and Kitty Dukakis. Dukakis is a member of the ReFormers Caucus of Issue One. He retired from Northeastern at age 90 in 2024, and the documentary film *Dukakis: Recipe for Democracy*, about his time as a professor at Northeastern, premiered on October 22, 2024. In August 2009, at age 75, Dukakis was mentioned as one of two leading candidates to serve as an interim U.S. Senator after Ted Kennedy's death; instead, Governor Patrick appointed Paul G. Kirk, the other candidate and favorite of the Kennedy family, to fill the seat. Dukakis has advocated for effective public transportation and high-speed rail to address automobile congestion and airport space limitations, as well as for an extended learning time initiative in public schools. On January 31, 2014, he stated he was not in favor of renaming South Station as the "Gov. Michael S. Dukakis Transportation Center," though it was later renamed to that name; he did not object to naming the as-yet unbuilt North-South Rail Link after him. In 2012, Dukakis supported Elizabeth Warren's successful U.S. Senate candidacy. During the 2016 Democratic presidential primaries, he endorsed Hillary Clinton. He endorsed Setti Warren's unsuccessful 2018 Massachusetts Democratic gubernatorial nomination and Elizabeth Warren's 2020 Democratic presidential campaign. He later endorsed Joe Biden in the general election and, with his wife, endorsed Ed Markey for reelection to his Massachusetts U.S. Senate seat in 2020 during both the primary and general elections. Dukakis was married to Kitty Dukakis (née Dickson) for 61 years, from June 20, 1963, until her death on March 21, 2025. Their first child, a daughter, died from anencephaly shortly after birth. They later had two daughters, Andrea and Kara. A son, John Dukakis (né Chaffetz), was born in 1958 to Kitty and her first husband, Phoenix businessman John Chaffetz (who later fathered former Congressman Jason Chaffetz); Michael Dukakis adopted John Jr. Dukakis is the cousin of Academy Award–winning actress Olympia Dukakis. In 1988, Michael and Kitty Dukakis said they attended both Greek Orthodox and Jewish worship services out of respect for both spouses' faiths. The Dukakises primarily lived in a home they bought in the early 1970s in Brookline, Massachusetts, and also maintained a home in Los Angeles during his teaching career at UCLA.
